Types of economic analyses Choose the most appropriate answer(s) for each item below 1. Choose TWO types of economic analyses which use an outcome measure that combines the duration and the health-related quality of life 2. Which ONE of the above approaches measures outcome in monetary terms? 3. Which ONE of the above approaches is most useful if the compared interventions are equally eff ective?

4. Which ONE of the above approaches uses a natural unidimensional clinical index of outcome? Explanation: Cost-minimization analysis is used when both interventions produce same outcome; hence just the costs are compared. Cost-eff ectiveness analysis is when both interventions result in an outcome that can be measured using same clinical scale (usually an one- dimensional index). Cost-utility analysis was developed to address the problem of conventional cost- eff ectiveness analysis, which did not allow decision-makers to compare the value of interventions for diff erent health problems. It is specifi cally used when the decision-maker has to consider the disease burden, side eff ects and social impact etc., in addition to clinical eff ectiveness. A composite measure of this aspect of health-related outcomes is called health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) measure health as a combination of the duration of life and the health-related quality of life (HRQoL). QALYs do not capture diff erences in the process characteristics of interventions (e.g. acceptability of a treatment, preferences of the individual), and there is substantial evidence that patients do attach value to these. Some have argued that due to this limitation of cost- utility analysis, health economists must provide a description of the costs of alternative interventions and a profi le of all the health and non-

health impacts of the interventions to the decision-makers. This is referred to as cost-consequences analysis. This can be used when two diff erent interventions with diff erent clinical outcomes are compared - as in cost benefi t analysis - but instead of simple conversion of outcome into money values, natural units (including QALYs) are given which can then be translated according to health preference states. (Adapted from McCabe, 2009: whatisseries, Bandolier website) Correct Answer is : 1. Cost utility analysis, Cost consequences analysis 2. Cost benefi t analysis 3. Cost minimization analysis 4. Cost eff ectiveness analysis

Psychometrics of rating scales Which of the listed terms best describes the attributes of the scales that are being tested in each of the following scenarios? 1. You are administering a putative test of cognition and MMSE (mini-mental state examination) at the same time, and the correlation between the two is computed 2. A new self-report questionnaire for PTSD called NEO-PTSD has questions covering the three major dimensions of PTSD - hyperarousal symptoms, avoidance and intrusions - in a detailed manner. 3. A medical student has noted that a specifi c scale has been repeatedly used in several controlled trials evaluating treatments for early onset schizophrenia. He is now keen to know the extent to which the observations using this scale can be generalized to a wider population of patients. 4. The extent to which the same trait is measured by diff erent methods 5. The extent to which an instrument distinguishes the various distinct constructs that may relate to each other 6. A research team wants to assess whether the acute stress disorder related dissociation in trauma-exposed youth accounts for later PTSD in adult life. Explanation: 1) Concurrent validity refl ects the agreement of a new instrument with another scale, which has itself been shown to be valid. It is usually determined by comparing the new scale within an external gold standard.
2) Content validity refers to whether the contents i.e. each sub-scales, items or elements of the test are in line with the general objectives or specifi cations the test was originally designed to measure. A good coverage of all domains thought to be related to the measured condition would improve the content validity of an instrument.
3) External validity describes the extent to which the results from a study can be generalized to a wider population.
4) When two instruments produce the same result, they are probably measuring the sae construct or trait; thus they are likely to be convergent.
5) If an instrument has good divergent validity, it will be able to accurately discriminate between overlapping constructs. For example, Hamilton Anxiety Scale will be said to have high divergent validity, if it rates symptoms seen in a patient with Generalised Anxiety Disorder consistently higher than the symptoms seen in a patient with depression and some features of anxiety. 6) When testing predictive validity, we assess an instrument's ability to predict something it should theoretically be able to predict. In this example, the authors expect dissociation to predict later PTSD.

stem: A 40-year-old man is a long term cocaine user. He is likely to have abnormalities in which of the following cognitive domains?
explanation: Being a stimulant, cocaine enhances cognitive functions, especially response inhibition and psychomotor processing speed, acutely after administration, though long-term use impairs cognition. 30% of dependent users and even 12% of recreational users exhibit clinically relevant cognitive impairment (see Vonmoos et al., 2014). The most impaired domains were sustained attention, response inhibition (impulsivity), verbal learning/memory, and working memory (Spronk et al., 2013). Abstinence helps to attain a level of cognitive performance level similar to non-users. Such recovery of cognition is not complete, as working memory impairments may continue despite 1-year of abstinence, especially in those who start cocaine use at an early age (Vonmoos et al., 2014).

Characterizing the cognitive eff ects of cocaine: a comprehensive review.Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 37(8), 1838-1859. 2. Vonmoos, M., Hulka, L. M., Preller, K. H., Minder, F., Baumgartner, M. R., & Quednow, B. B. (2014). stem: Which of the following substance, even when used concurrently with clozapine, does not aff ect the metabolism of clozapine?
explanation: Dose adjustments are often necessary when certain medications are used concurrently with clozapine. CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g.,fl uvoxamine or ciprofl oxacin [strong], oral contraceptives or caff eine [moderate]); CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., escitalopram, erythromycin, paroxetine, bupropion,fl uoxetine, duloxetine [moderate], sertraline or diazepam [weak]) can increase adverse eff ects associated with clozapine's by aff ecting its breakdown. With strong inhibitors, it is advisable to initiate with one-third of the usual clozapine dose and titrate slowly. If these ' CYP inhibitors' are discontinued during clozapine treatment, then clozapine dose must be increased; else its therapeutic eff ectiveness could be lost. CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort, and rifampin) or CYP1A2 inducers (e.g., tobacco smoking) can increase clozapine metabolism and thus reduce eff ectiveness. If these agents are used, clozapine dose should be increased to achieve the same therapeutic eff ect. If these are discontinued during clozapine treatment, then clozapine dose must be reduced, else dose-related adverse eff ects associated with clozapine will become more pronounced. Please note that it is the tar in cigarettes that induce CYP1A2 activity, not nicotine. Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) does not usually aff ect clozapine levels. Ref: https://www.pharma.us.novartis.com/product/pi/pdf/Clozaril.pdf http://www0.health.nsw.gov.au/pubs/2012/pdf/tool_03_clozapine_smoking_cessation.pdf

explanation: About 80 per cent of alcoholic patients recovering from Wernicke's encephalopathy develop Korsakoff 's amnesic syndrome. It is characterized by marked defi cits in anterograde and to some extent retrograde episodic memory, apathy, an intact sensorium, and relative preservation of other intellectual abilities such as attention, procedural memory and working memory. Confabulation occurs due to a double lesion – frontal defi cits and diencephalic defi cits. In terms of treatment, continue oral thiamine replacement for up to 2 years.

stem: Which one among the following test is a specifi c biomarker for heavy alcohol misuse?
explanation: Carbohydrate Defi cient Transferrin (CDT) is a biomarker for heavy alcohol consumption. The Carbohydrate Defi cient Transferrin (CDT) test is a particularly specifi c in tracking heavy alcohol consumption over an extended period of time. The advantage of using CDT in testing for alcohol misuse is it is unaff ected by mild alcohol related liver disease or fatty liver (due to obesity, diabetes etc) which can falsely increase γ- glutamyl transferase (GGT), the enzyme in blood most commonly used to indicate excess alcohol consumption. CDT is also unaff ected by chronic disease or B12/folate defi ciencies which can increase the mean corpuscular volume (MCV), another blood test used to detect alcohol misuse. Transferrin remains in the circulation for 7 to 14 days and CDT, therefore, can give an indication of alcohol consumption over this period of time, which gives it an advantage over blood or urine alcohol measurements, which only remain elevated for 24-48 hours after alcohol consumption. (Bergström, J.P. and Helander, A., 2008. Alcohol and alcoholism, 43(4), pp.436-441.)

stem: Which of the following is a helpful sign of distinguishing non-epileptiform attack disorder (NEAD) from epilepsy?
options: Resistance to eye opening during the seizure
correctAnswer: Resistance to eye opening during the seizure
explanation: Eyes may be kept tightly shut and resistance to eye opening occur during a pseudoseizure or non epileptiform attack disorder while during true seizures eyes are more often open. Pelvic thrusting movements are often regarded as a sign of non epileptiform attacks, but such movements can be seen in epileptic seizures, either during tonic-clonic convulsions or with complex partial seizures. Pelvic movements in tonic-clonic convulsions are more likely to be retropulsive, however, whereas those associated with non epileptiform attacks are usually propulsive. Elevations in serum prolactin occur in the postictal phase (20 to 25 minutes after the seizure subsides) after some types of epileptic seizures. The most consistent increase is found after generalized tonic-clonic convulsions.

stem: Which of the following is the best-recommended treatment option for a breastfeeding mother who is opiate dependent and requires interventions?
explanation: For methadone, breastfeeding can reduce the severity and duration of neonatal withdrawal (or abstinence) syndrome and delay the onset of symptoms. One reason for this can be the comfort obtained through mother/child bonding, another, the oral bioavailability of methadone. As a result of breast-feeding under methadone maintenance, the need for medical treatment of neonatal withdrawal syndrome may be decreased (compared to i.v. heroin use in the mother). If women want to breastfeed and no contraindication such as either infectious disease or continued illicit drug use exists, physicians should support their needs. The safety of buprenorphine in breastfeeding has not been well-investigated. So far, data available show low concentrations in breast milk so that a similar recommendation might be valid as for methadone. [Unger et al., Obstet Gynecol Int. 2012;2012:195954. doi: 10.1155/2012/195954.]

stem: In borderline personality disorder which of the following features will improve on its own after two years?
explanation: In McLean Study of Adult Development, the 24 symptoms of borderline personality disorder studied were classifi ed as acute and temperamental where acute symptoms are seen as akin to the positive symptoms of schizophrenia (most dramatic, leads to service consumption but may resolve relatively rapidly and are the best markers for the disorder), while the temperamental symptoms (innate but not immutable, resolve more slowly, and are not specifi c to borderline personality disorder but closely associated with ongoing psychosocial impairment) are seen as akin to negative symptoms. "Among the symptoms studied, the prevalence offi ve core borderline symptoms was found to decline with particular rapidity: quasi-psychotic thought, self-mutilation, help-seeking suicide eff orts, treatment regressions, and countertransference problems. In contrast, feelings of depression, anger, and loneliness/emptiness were the most stable symptoms" (Retrieved from http://ajp.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/ajp.2007.164.6.929).

explanation: In seasonal aff ective disorder many patients exhibit a seasona pattern to their illness. The classic presentation is of depression with reversed biological features in winter. There is often evidence of a bipolar 2 course with mild hypomania in spring or summer.

stem: Which of the following is true concerning restless legs syndrome?
options: Use of benzodiazepines must be avoided
More common in people with Lewy Body dementia
Patients often complain of deep prolonged sleep
correctAnswer: More common in people with Lewy Body dementia
explanation: In the majority of cases, RLS is idiopathic and may run in families. Some cases of RLS are caused by iron defi ciency anemia; RLS is often linked to Parkinson,s or Lewy Body Dementia in the elderly (some studies suggest up to 10% of patients with DLB may have RLS). Evidence pointing towards a link includes response to dopaminergic agents in both DLB/PD and RLS, and an association of RLS with the parkin mutation.

stem: Which of the following can explain the diff erence in outcome between developed and developing nations in schizophrenia?
explanation: International Study of Schizophrenia - WHO ISoS (1997) was a follow-up analysis that included two major WHO incidence cohorts. Thefi rst cohort was part of IPSS - International pilot study of schizophrenia while the second cohort was from the Determinants of Outcome of Severe Mental Disorder and the reduction of disability study (DOSMeD) which followed IPSS with more rigorous method and outcome measurement. IPSS assessed 1,202 persons diagnosed with schizophrenia in nine countries. The results showed that persons with schizophrenia in the 'developing' world (g., Columbia, India, Nigeria) had better outcomes than persons in the developed countries (g., Moscow, London, Washington, Prague, Aarhus and Denmark). In total 52% of persons in the developing countries were assessed to be in the best outcome category (defi ned as a single episode only, followed by full or partial recovery) compared with 39% in the developed countries. In a 5-year follow-up 73% of those participants from the developing world were in the best outcome group compared with 52% in the developed world. DOSMeD used more rigorous criteria and followed more than 1,300 patients in 10 countries and, similar to the IPSS, discovered that the highest rates of recovery occurred in the developing world. At a 2-year follow-up, 56% of those in the developing world were in the best outcome group compared to 39% of the participants from the developed countries. DOSMeD excluded mode of onset being a confounding factor. Diff erential follow-up rates, diff erential outcome measures, diff erential sex and age distribution, diagnostic ambiguities did not confound the above results as proved later by Hopper and Wanderling (Scz Bulletin 2000; 26, 835-46)

stem: The correct answer is: None of the listed Which among the following is a good prognostic factor in schizophrenia?
explanation: Acute onset (sudden onset) is a good prognostic factor in terms of predicting the outcome of schizophrenia. Poor outcome is associated with younger age of onset, male sex, poor premorbid functioning and persistence of negative symptoms (defi cit syndrome). There is also evidence that the duration of psychotic symptoms prior to treatment correlates with time to remission and level of remission (Marshall et al 2005)

stem: Which drug used in relapse prevention and maintaining abstinence from alcohol requires acute monitoring?
explanation: Disulfi ram blocks the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase, which results in the accumulation of acetaldehyde. This leads to signs and symptoms such asfl ushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol is consumed. This reaction is dose- dependent and if a large amount of alcohol is consumed, a more severe reaction may ensue leading to hypertension, collapse and even death. Its aim is to act as a deterrent. Witnessing or supervising the taking of Disulfi ram is important for its effi cacy.

stem: Which of the following class of drugs increases the risk of cardiac malformation in foetus?
explanation: SSRIs like Paroxetine has been specifi cally associated with cardiac malformations, particularly after high dose (> 25 mg/day),fi rst trimester exposure.

stem: Which of the following cognitive domains is most impaired in patients with schizophrenia?
explanation: According to MATRICS consensus battery, the most important cognitive domains with a defi cit in schizophrenia are working memory, attention/vigilance, verbal learning and memory, visual learning and memory, reasoning and problem solving, speed of processing, and social cognition (Green et al. 2004). While there are some discrepancies in the literature as to the magnitude of eff ect sizes of defi cits in individual domains, meta-analytic results based on several studies suggest that the most severe impairment is seen in processing speed (ES=1.25), followed by episodic verbal memory (ES = 1.23). Most other domains showed medium to large sized defi cits (ES 0.63 to 1.11) (Schaefer et al., 2013) Ref: Green MF, Kern RS, Heaton RK. Longitudinal studies of cognition and functional outcome in schizophrenia: implications for MATRICS. Schizophr Res. 2004;72(1):41-51. Schaefer, J., Giangrande, E., Weinberger, D. R., & Dickinson, D. (2013). The global cognitive impairment in schizophrenia: consistent over decades and around the world. Schizophrenia research, 150(1), 42-50.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a degenerative condition?
explanation: Neurodegeneration is a common term used for the progressive loss of structure or function of neurons, including death of neurons. Conditions like Alzheimer's disease, Huntington disease, Multisystem atrophy and Parkinson's disease occur as a result of neurodegenerative processes. Such diseases are incurable, resulting in progressive degeneration and/or death of neuron cells. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an organ-specifi c autoimmune disease targeting central nervous system myelin.

stem: Which of the following is the best treatment of choice in a child with Post traumatic stress disorder?
explanation: The treatment of a child with Post traumatic stress disorder(PTSD) relies on psychological therapies. Trauma focussed Cognitive Behavioural therapy, adapted to the age and developmental stage of the child or young person is one of the best interventions for PTSD in children. EMDR (Eye movement desensitisation reprocessing) has been shown to be a useful adjunct to psychological therapies for young victims of trauma.

stem: Which of the following is the commonest co-morbidity seen in patients with borderline personality disorder?
explanation: The most common co-morbidity seen in patients with borderline personality disorder is a mood disorder (96%). Among them, depressive disorder is seen in 71-83% of patients. Any anxiety disorder is seen in 88% of patients. (Ref: Piskin & Paris, Co-morbidities in Borderline personality disorder. http://www.psychiatrictimes.com/borderline-personality/comorbidities-borderline-personality-disorder)

stem: Which of the following medications should be stopped prior to giving ECT?
explanation: Nitrazepam is a type of Benzodiazepine. Benzodiazepines (BDZ) may inhibit ECT effi cacy by 2 mechanisms: the raising of seizure threshold and the inhibition of seizure propagation. Therefore it is best to be avoid them prior to giving ECT

stem: Which of the following set of symptoms are common in patients with post concussional syndrome?

Episodic memory loss along with subtle personality changes
explanation: Post-concussional syndrome is characterised by headache; dizziness; insomnia; irritability; complaints of slowed thinking; emotional lability; increased sensitivity to noise, light, etc.; fatigue; poor concentration; anxiety; and depression.

stem: Which of the following statements is true about REM sleep disorder?

It occurs during the early part of the night
It is seen normally in 50% of old age adults
In REM sleep disorder, there is loss of muscle tone
correctAnswer: It is associated with Lewy body dementia
explanation: Normally REM sleep is associated with loss of muscle tone and dreaming. In RBD, there is no loss of muscle tone and the dreams are acted as complex behaviours.Patients act out their dreams, with limited awareness of surroundings. The episodes arise during the middle to latter third of the night during REM sleep. It is associated with disorders such as Parkinson's disease, diff use Lewy body disease, multiple system atrophy and Gullian–Barre syndrome. Treatment with clonazepam has been shown to be eff ective.

stem: Which of the following tools is used to screen personality disorder as per diagnostic descriptions?
explanation: The Personality Diagnostic Questionnaire (PDQ) is an eff ective screening tool for the presence of personality disorders. It is made of 100 true or false questions that are structured to align with the personality diagnoses described by the DSM-IV diagnostic criteria for the axis II disorders.

stem: You are reviewing a 52-year-old lady with paranoid schizophrenia who requires medical treatment for her symptoms. She has a history of breast cancer. Which of the following would be the LEAST appropriate medication to prescribe her?
explanation: Treatment with amisulpride can induce hyperprolactinaemia, a long-term consequence of which is a possible increase in the risk of breast cancer. The antipsychotics that are not usually associated with hyperprolactinaemia include Aripiprazole, Olanzapine, Quetiapine and Clozapine (for more details see SPMM Smart Revise Notes)

stem: Anorexia nervosa in adulthood is most commonly associated with which of the following?
explanation: Anorexia nervosa is most commonly associated with obsessive and other anxious personality traits.

stem: Which one among the following is a signifi cant risk factor for the development of Neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
explanation: Risk factors for NMS: High ambient temperature, dehydration, patient agitation or catatonia, rapid antipsychotic initiation/dose escalation, withdrawal of anti-parkinsonian medication, use of high potency agents/depot IM preparations, history of organic brain disease such as dementia, history of aff ective disorder, previous history of NMS, Predisposing drugs like lithium and anticholinergic medications. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry-882)

stem: Severe lithium toxicity presents with which of the following signs?
explanation: Central Nervous System features of severe lithium toxicity: Blackout spells, epileptiform seizures, slurred speech, dizziness, vertigo, incontinence of urine or feces, somnolence, psychomotor retardation, restlessness, confusion, stupor, coma, acute dystonia, downbeat nystagmus. (Ref: McKnight RF, et al. Lithium toxicity profi le: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. 2012 Mar 2;379(9817):721-8.)

stem: Mary is a 42-year-old woman with bipolar disorder with frequent depressive episodes. What drug would you choose as the best prophylaxis against depression?

explanation: Intrusive thoughts that cause anxiety are a feature of OCD, and there is a greater predisposition to this distressing experience following a traumatic birth.

stem: What side eff ect would you monitor closely in a patient taking Donepezil?
explanation: Acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors (AChEs) like Donepezil may have vagotonic eff ects on heart rate leading to bradycardia. AChE inhibitors can induce sinus bradycardia, sino-atrial block, and aggravate pre-existing sinus node disease and atrioventricular block (Savie et al, 1998). Donepezil overdose has been reported to result in profound sinus bradycardia that can be reversed with atropine (Shepherd et al, 1999; Hidetaka et al, 2003). Therefore it is important to monitor for signs like bradycardia.

stem: Which of the following psychotic disorders with onset in childhood has the worst prognosis?
explanation: There is limited data on recovery rates from childhood onset schizophrenia but given that the emergence of the disorder disrupts psychosocial development and schooling. It is unsurprising the very early onset schizophrenia and early onset schizophrenia often has a relatively poor prognosis even with psychopharmacological treatment. 80-90% will have 2 or more episodes in a 5-year period. Presence of aff ective symptoms off ers a better outcome.

stem: A teenager attends the CAMHS clinic for sleep problems and noted to have poor sleep hygiene. Which of the following advice should be given as a sleep hygiene measure?
options: Try to do strenuous exercise in the 4 hours before bedtime

Having a cold bath 1-2 hours before bedtime
correctAnswer: Avoid large meals prior to bed
explanation: "A healthy, balanced diet will help you to sleep well, but timing is important. Some peoplefi nd that a very empty stomach at bedtime is distracting, so it can be useful to have a light snack, but a heavy meal soon before bed can also interrupt sleep. Only try to sleep when you actually feel tired or sleepy, rather than spending too much time awake in bed. Even if you have a bad night sleep and are tired it is important that you try to keep your daytime activities the same as you had planned. That is, don't avoid activities because you feel tired. This can reinforce the insomnia. Having a hot bath 1-2 hours before bedtime can be useful, as it will raise your body temperature, causing you to feel sleepy as your body temperature drops again". (Excerpt from: www.cci.health.wa.gov.au Also see: Tan E, et al. BMC pediatrics. 2012 Dec 7;12(1):1.)

stem: In which of the following therapies diagrammatic reformulations are used to represent the reciprocal roles that are dominant in one's relationships with others?
explanation: Cognitive analytical therapy (CAT) usually lasts for 8-24, but usually 12 weekly sessions. Reformulation letters are addressed to the patient written by the therapist (4th session). These letters will give a description of the presenting problems and also illustrate the present situation using a series of Target Problem Procedures which may be drawn as a diagram (also known as an SDR, or sequential diagrammatic reformulation). These show how the situations experienced in the past still infl uence one's current behaviour. Gat conclusion of the therapy, both the therapist and the patient write good-bye letters summarising progress and formally closing the relationship.

stem: Which of the following treatments was specifi cally developed to reduce intentional self-harm behaviour?
explanation: M. Linehan developed 'dialectical behavioral therapy' to treat chronically suicidal borderline patients. DBT rests on a biosocial model (Borderline personality is a disorder in the regulation of emotions and stress tolerance). The numerous dysfunctional patterns of behaviour such as self-destructive behaviour, impulsivity and severe dissociative phenomena are regarded as futile problem-solving attempts. This concept focuses on the continuing balance between the necessity of accepting maladaptive behaviour patterns in both an intra psychic and an interactional context while still working to change them.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has a history of repeated self-harm and multiple unstable relationships culminating in suicide attempts. She is very demanding and diffi cult to treat according to the community mental health team involved in treating her. Which of the following modalities may be suitable?
explanation: DBT was introduced to reduce self-harm in borderline patients. Marsha Linehan is the major proponent. The four modes of treatment in DBT are (1) group skills training, (2) individual therapy, (3) phone consultations, and (4) consultation team. Key Techniques (remember DICE) are Distress tolerance includes accepting,fi nding meaning for, and tolerating distress. This includes crisis survival strategies such as distracting, self-soothing, improving the moment, and thinking of pros and cons and acceptance skills such as radical acceptance, turning the mind toward acceptance, and willingness versus willfulness. Interpersonal eff ectiveness training is very similar to assertiveness and problem-solving training. Core mindfulness training - learning to monitor internal mental states. Emotion regulation skills form an important part of DBT.

explanation: The PICO process is a technique used in evidence based practice to frame and answer a clinical or health care related question. stem: You are a busy inpatient consultant formulating clinical guidelines for your Trust. You need to determine which antidepressant your department should use asfi rst-line treatment in depression. Which of the following should you perform?
explanation: The most appropriate of these is likely to be a literature review, which is an analysis of current knowledge including substantivefi ndings. A busy inpatient consultant is unlikely to have the time or resources to conduct a meta-analysis. This is a statistical analysis that combines the results of multiple scientifi c studies. A randomised controlled trial involves comparing various interventions against one another, often in a double blind fashion. A case-control study involves identifying individuals who have experienced a particular outcome and then matching them to controls by demographic and other relevant factors, before determining whether the aff ected individuals were more likely to have encountered an earlier exposure. An audit is a comparison of existing practice against an established standard.

stem: A study linking patient registers of isotretinoin users (1980-9) to hospital and death registers (1980-2001) was conducted in Sweden. 5756 patients aged 15 to 49 years prescribed isotretinoin for severe acne observed for 17,197 person-years before, 2905 person-years during, and 87,120 person-years after treatment. Standardised incidence ratio (observed number divided by expected number of suicide attempts standardised by sex, age, and calendar year), calculated up to three years before, during, and up to 15 years after end of treatment. 128 patients were admitted to hospital for attempted suicide. Between three years and one year before the start of treatment, the standardised incidence ratios, comparing the study cohort with the general population, gradually rose from 0.89 (95% confi dence interval 0.54 to 1.37) three years before treatment to 1.36 (0.65 to 2.50) in the year before treatment forfi rst attempts and from 0.99 (0.65 to 1.44) three years before treatment to 1.57 (0.86 to 2.63) in the year preceding treatment for all attempts. The risks were highest within six months after the start of treatment: 1.93 (1.08 to 3.18) forfi rst attempts and 1.78 (1.04 to 2.85) for all attempts. The standardised incidence ratios then decreased, and the number of observed attempts was close to the expected number within three years after treatment: standardised incidence ratio 0.97 (0.64 to 1.40) forfi rst attempts and 1.04 (0.74 to 1.43) for all attempts Twelve (38%) of 32 patients who made theirfi rst suicide attempt before treatment made a new attempt or committed suicide thereafter. In contrast, 10 (71%) of the 14 who made theirfi rst suicide attempt within six months after treatment stopped made a new attempt or committed suicide during follow-up (two sample test of proportions, P=0.034). Patients with a history of suicide attempts before treatment made new attempts to a lesser extent than did patients who started such behaviour in connection with treatment. An increased risk of attempted suicide was apparent up to six months after the end of treatment with isotretinoin, which motivates a close monitoring of patients for suicidal behaviour for up to a year after treatment has ended. However, from this data, an additional risk due to the isotretinoin treatment cannot be established. Ref: Sundström et al. BMJ 2010; 341 :c5812 http://www.bmj.com/content/341/bmj.c5812. What type of research has been reported here?
explanation: This study identifi ed an exposure cohort - i.e people exposed to isotretinoin prescription for acne, using a case register and collected retrospective data on the outcome of interest from linked registers (suicide attempts). The authors initially standardised the incidence rates of attempted suicides using general population rates recorded in the same time period. But instead of comparing them with a non-exposed matched cohort, the researchers undertook an internal comparison of incidence rates before, during and after the exposure. This is sometimes termed a cohort-crossover analysis (same cohort is used as both exposed and unexposed group, but at diff erent time points).

Between three years and one year before the start of treatment, the standardised incidence ratios, comparing the study cohort with the general population, gradually rose from 0.89 (95% confi dence interval 0.54 to 1.37) three years before treatment to 1.36 (0.65 to 2.50) in the year before treatment forfi rst attempts and from 0.99 (0.65 to 1.44) three years before treatment to 1.57 (0.86 to 2.63) in the year preceding treatment for all attempts. The risks were highest within six months after the start of treatment: 1.93 (1.08 to 3.18) forfi rst attempts and 1.78 (1.04 to 2.85) for all attempts. The standardised incidence ratios then decreased, and the number of observed attempts was close to the expected number within three years after treatment: standardised incidence ratio 0.97 (0.64 to 1.40) forfi rst attempts and 1.04 (0.74 to 1.43) for all attempts Twelve (38%) of 32 patients who made theirfi rst suicide attempt before treatment made a new attempt or committed suicide thereafter. In contrast, 10 (71%) of the 14 who made theirfi rst suicide attempt within six months after treatment stopped made a new attempt or committed suicide during follow-up (two sample test of proportions, P=0.034). Patients with a history of suicide attempts before treatment made new attempts to a lesser extent than did patients who started such behaviour in connection with treatment. An increased risk of attempted suicide was apparent up to six months after the end of treatment with isotretinoin, which motivates a close monitoring of patients for suicidal behaviour for up to a year after treatment has ended. However, from this data, an additional risk due to the isotretinoin treatment cannot be established. Ref: Sundström et al. BMJ 2010; 341 :c5812 http://www.bmj.com/content/341/bmj.c5812. When comparing the standardised rates before 1 year and after 6 months of treatment, there was no statistically signifi cant diff erence in the rates offi rst attempts of suicide. From the data presented here, the best possible explanation for this observation is
options: Suicidal risk may be infl uenced by the severity of acne rather than the use of isotretinoin
First attempt of suicide is a very common event, with high rates even in the general population
Prior antibiotic treatment, rather than isotretinoin, is associated with risk of suicide
Treatment with isotretinoin reduces the risk of attempted suicide
Isotretinoin is not associated with elevated suicidal risk
correctAnswer: Suicidal risk may be infl uenced by the severity of acne rather than the use of isotretinoin
explanation: Given the trend of increased incidence rates among those with severe acne that started even before the exposure began, we have grounds to suspect that suicidal risk may be infl uenced by the severity of acne rather than the use of isotretinoin.

stem: The attached chart was presented along with the results reported from BALANCE study, in which 330 patients aged 16 years and older with bipolar I disorder from 41 sites in the UK, France, USA, and Italy were randomly allocated to open-label lithium monotherapy (plasma concentration 0.4-1.0 mmol/L, n=110), valproate monotherapy (750-1250 mg, n=110), or both agents in combination (n=110), after an active run-in of 4-8 weeks on the combination. The investigators and participants were informed of treatment allocation. All outcome events were considered by the trial management team, who were masked to the treatment assignment. Participants were followed up for up to 24 months. The primary outcome was initiation of new intervention for an emergent mood episode. The run-in phase was used in order to:
options: cacy rates of lithium and valproate combination
increase the sample size for primary analysis
confi ne randomization to those who are likely to complete the 2-year study
improve the generalisability of the results
correctAnswer: confi ne randomization to those who are likely to complete the 2-year study
explanation: Run-in phases are useful to stratify or select a clinical sample that has the potential to adhere to the prescribed treatment in an RCT. This improves the internal validity and reduces attrition bias, though reduces the overall number of patients entering randomisation. As acknowledged by the authors of this paper "use of an active run-in means that the randomised sample was a selected group, and hence the results are most applicable to patients who can tolerate treatment with lithium and valproate and who are largely adherent to therapy". Thus the run-in phase has reduced the generalisability, but has improved the internal validity by reducing drop-outs after randomisation.

stem: A patient with chronic schizophrenia is being considered for rehousing in one of the two rehabilitation units available in the city. Home A is known to provide an average of 0.5 QALY per patient at the end of 1-year placement at a cost of £900 per week per patient. Home B is known to provide an average gain of 0.7 QALY per patient at a cost of £1100 per week per patient after the same length of placement. What is the incremental cost incurred if Home B is chosen instead of Home A?
explanation: In this example, the incremental cost is £1100 minus £900 each week for 52 weeks for 1 year of placement. In other words, the incremental cost is £200 x 52 = £10400.

Home B is known to provide an average gain of 0.7 QALY per patient at a cost of £1100 per week per patient after the same length of placement. What is the incremental cost per 1 QALY gain when using home B instead of home A?
explanation: ICER is given by the ratio between incremental cost and incremental eff ectiveness. In this example, the incremental cost is £1100 minus £900 each week for 52 weeks for 1 year of placement. In other words, the incremental cost is £200 x 52 = £10400. This investment can only bring about a diff erence of 0.7-0.5 = 0.2 QALY improvement. For 1 QALY improvement, the cost would be 5 times larger i.e., £10400 * 5 = £52000. That is, ICER = dC/ dE = [( £1100-£900)*52]/(0.7-0.5) = £200*52/0.2 = £52000
